 OpenAI might rebrand its data centers as ‘AI compute campuses’ 
 Data centers are deeply unpopular . But what if we called them something else? 
 Axios reports that OpenAI is preparing a “PR blitz” for after the midterm elections on Tuesday, as Democrats seem likely to win back the House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate, too . 
 The company’s chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane told Axios that the midterms will be “a bit of a movie trailer for what you’re going to see in 2028,” when he expects AI to be “ the issue” in the presidential election. 
 So OpenAI is to influence the AI debate moving forward, with Lehane discussing several proposals, including the development of AI “speed limits” ; finding ways to help people see AI as empowering them in their daily lives; pushing the U.S. to take a role in developing global standards — and yes, rebranding data centers as “AI compute campuses.” 
 Lehane also described the conversation around data centers (a debate that has pushed Amazon and Microsoft to say they will no longer use NDAs in their negotiations with local governments ) as “good and healthy.” 
 “Communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they really and truly get a transformative benefit from these projects,” he said.

 Dazzle AI CEO Marissa Mayer recently became the latest tech CEO to face criticism over seemingly out-of-touch comments extolling the usefulness of AI. 
 In Mayer’s case, that involved asking an AI tool for help with a school-assigned description of her daughter . For OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, that’s included suggesting that parents create personalized podcasts for their kids’ drive to school and also declaring that he could not imagine parenting without ChatGPT . Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has even suggested that it will become increasingly acceptable to meet your social and romantic needs through AI . 
 This all led TechCrunch’s Amanda Silberling to wonder if AI executives are simply too out-of-touch to build products for normal people — a crucial question with Anthropic set to go public just as Wall Street begins losing its appetite for heavy AI spending . 
 On the latest episode of the Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I chatted with Amanda about why industry leaders can sometimes seem so tone deaf. Kirsten wondered if this is more of a marketing problem or a product problem.  
 Amanda’s answer: “A little bit of both.” She also argued that the tech industry is increasingly pushing a future “where basic human interaction gets more and more optimized out of actually occurring,” adding, “And call me old school, but I think that humans being able to talk to each other is probably a net positive for society.”

 DeepSeek open-sources Super-Agent, a coding agent that watches team chats for work 
 Deepseek released a research prototype of dsh-superagent, a coding agent that does work on a GitHub repository for you. 
 Who can ask for work 
 The agent gets to work in two situations: an allowed user asks for something, or a rule your team wrote covers it. You can also open up a chat or GitHub scope, and then anyone in it can request work just by mentioning the agent. A message, comment or quoted document can’t expand what the agent is allowed to do, since the host is the one enforcing the lists and rules. 
 By default, requests that aren’t explicit, such as an unaddressed message, a bot’s message or an unlisted person’s follow-up, are assessed and recorded as ones the agent would have accepted, but none is accepted. Explicit requests, such as an allowed user mentioning the agent, work in every mode. The advice is to switch to auto after you’ve reviewed those records. 
 Merging 
 A prompt called Delivery requirements controls auto-merge, and the host adds no merge logic of its own. By default the agent doesn’t turn on auto-merge under its own account, because GitHub credits the merge to whoever enabled it. Unless the prompt names another account for merging, people merge. 
 dsh-superagent is available for free on GitHub .

 2. November 2026 
 Anthropic hat kurz vor seinem geplanten Börsengang neue Geschäftszahlen vorgelegt und rutscht operativ wieder ins Minus. Laut Bloomberg lag der Quartalsumsatz bei knapp 17 Milliarden Dollar , zwölfmal so viel wie ein Jahr zuvor. Die Betriebskosten von 17,5 Milliarden Dollar lagen jedoch über dem Umsatz, im Vorquartal hatte Anthropic laut The Information noch Gewinn gemacht. Unter dem Strich steht ein Quartalsverlust von 23,3 Milliarden Dollar, nach 12,1 Milliarden ein Jahr zuvor. 
 Als Gründe für den Anstieg nennt Anthropic fünf Milliarden Dollar für kurzfristig gesicherte Rechenkapazität und zwei Milliarden, mit denen es Spenden seiner Beschäftigten verdoppelte. Der Engpass bei Rechenleistung beschäftigt Anthropic seit Ende vergangenen Jahres. Laut New York Times schloss das Unternehmen seither Dutzende Verträge mit Amazon, Google, SpaceX, Chipherstellern und früheren Krypto-Minern. Dieses Jahr soll Anthropic über mehr als 3,5 Gigawatt verfügen, nächstes Jahr will es die Menge verdoppeln. 
 Insgesamt hat es sich laut aktualisiertem Prospekt zu 895 Milliarden Dollar für Rechenleistung und Rechenzentrumsmieten verpflichtet. Diese Kosten erhöhen laut New York Times den Druck auf den Börsengang, der rund 100 Milliarden Dollar bringen könnte. Bis zu 3,5 Milliarden Dollar davon sollen von japanischen Anlegern kommen. Anthropic’s quarterly revenue jumps to $17B, losses grow ahead of IPO - SiliconANGLE

 UPDATED 18:19 EST / NOVEMBER 02 2026

 Anthropic’s quarterly revenue jumps to $17B, losses grow ahead of IPO 
 by Maria Deutscher 
 Anthropic PBC today published an updated version of the S-1 filing for its upcoming public offering. 
 The original document, which the company released last Monday, didn’t contain its third-quarter financial results. The new version reveals that Anthropic generated $17 billion in revenue during the three months ended Sept. 30. That’s more than 11 times more than what it made a year earlier, but represents a deacceleration in quarter-over-quarter growth. Anthropic’s top line grew 47% on a quarterly basis, down from 144% three months earlier. 
 The artificial intelligence provider faces multipronged competition from open-source models, OpenAI Group PBC and tech giants such as Google LLC. The Alphabet Inc.’s newest model, Gemini 4 Carbon, outperforms Claude Opus 5.5 across multiple benchmarks. 
 Anthropic is investing heavily in training infrastructure to stay ahead of the competition. The company took a $5 billion charge in the third quarter because demand for computing hardware was higher than expected, which required it to purchase hardware at a premium. Hardware bought on short notice is more expensive than Anthropic’s usual capacity commitments, which it books 12 to 18 months before they’re needed. 
 The AI provider also took a $2 billion charge in connection with its non-cash employee donation matching program. That left Anthropic with a $536 million operating loss at the end of the third quarter. Three months earlier, it posted $974 million in operating income. Anthropic’s adjusted operating income, which excludes stock-based compensation and charitable contributions, jumped by $300 million on a quarterly basis to $2.5 billion. 
 The company had $895.4 billion in outstanding infrastructure commitments as of Sept 30.
